questions.stem: Which is an example of a point source of water pollution?
options: Pesticide spray drifting on the wind across a wide area of cropland
Wastewater discharged from a factory's outlet pipe into a creek
Fertiliser washed off many farms across a catchment after rain
Oil and rubber washed off city roads by stormwater run-off
questions.explanation: A point source is a single, identifiable discharge point, such as a pipe or chimney. Run-off from many farms or roads comes from a large area with no single outlet, so it is a diffuse (non-point) source and much harder to regulate.

questions.stem: Ground-level ozone in photochemical smog is described as a secondary pollutant because it:
options: forms in the air when other pollutants react in sunlight
is emitted directly from car exhausts and factory chimneys
is less harmful to human health than the primary pollutants
is released by natural sources rather than by human activity
questions.explanation: Ozone is not emitted directly; it forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight. A primary pollutant, such as nitrogen dioxide from exhausts, is emitted directly from its source.

questions.stem: Why are PM2.5 particles generally more harmful to human health than PM10 particles?
options: Their large size lets them block the airways and stop air reaching the lungs
They are always made of toxic metals, while PM10 is only harmless dust
They dissolve in rain droplets and fall out of the air long before PM10 can do so
Their small size lets them travel deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream
questions.explanation: PM2.5 particles are 2.5 µm or smaller in diameter, so they slip past the nose and upper airways into the alveoli, and some pass into the blood. Larger PM10 particles are mostly trapped higher in the respiratory tract. Particle composition varies for both sizes.

questions.stem: On a cold, still winter morning, smoke from wood heaters in a valley town stays close to the ground instead of rising. Which condition explains this?
options: A temperature inversion, with a layer of warmer air above cooler surface air
A temperature inversion, with a layer of cooler air above warmer surface air
Strong winds pushing the smoke down from the hills into the valley floor
High humidity making the smoke particles heavier so they sink to the ground
questions.explanation: Normally air cools with height, so warm polluted air rises and disperses. In an inversion, a warm layer sits over cold surface air and acts as a lid, trapping smoke near the ground. Still conditions, not strong winds, allow the inversion to persist.

questions.stem: Pesticide A is highly soluble in water. Pesticide B is insoluble in water but soluble in fat. Which prediction is most likely?
options: Neither will enter food chains, because pesticides are broken down as soon as they are applied
A is more likely to leach into groundwater; B is more likely to build up in animal tissue
A is more likely to build up in animal tissue; B is more likely to leach into groundwater
Both are equally likely to leach, because solubility does not affect how pollutants move
questions.explanation: Water-soluble chemicals move with water, so they can leach through soil or wash into waterways, but they are also excreted more easily. Fat-soluble chemicals are stored in fatty tissue rather than excreted, so they accumulate in organisms and food chains.

questions.stem: A coal-fired power station raises the height of its chimney. What is the main effect on its sulfur dioxide pollution?
options: Emissions are concentrated closer to the plant, raising local exposure
Emissions are converted into harmless gases before they leave the stack
Emissions are spread over a wider area, but the total emitted is unchanged
Emissions are reduced overall, because less sulfur dioxide is produced
questions.explanation: A taller stack releases gases higher, where winds disperse them further and dilute them before they reach the ground nearby. The same amount of sulfur dioxide is still produced, so it can still form acid rain further downwind.

questions.stem: Which pair of gases are the main causes of acid rain?
options: Nitrogen and argon
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides
Carbon monoxide and methane from vehicles
Ozone and chlorofluorocarbons
questions.explanation: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides react with water in the atmosphere to form sulfuric and nitric acids. Carbon dioxide makes natural rain slightly acidic, but it is not the main cause of acid rain.

questions.stem: A bushfire and a vehicle factory both release pollutants to the air. Which statement is correct?
options: Natural sources only release gases, never particulate matter
Bushfire smoke disperses only within the burnt area itself
Pollutants can come from both natural and manufactured sources
Only manufactured sources release pollutants that harm health
questions.explanation: Bushfires, volcanoes, dust storms and pollen are natural sources of air pollutants, and bushfire smoke can carry fine particles hundreds of kilometres. Many health effects of smoke particles are similar whatever their source.

questions.stem: The gradual build-up of a pollutant in an organism's tissues over its lifetime, because it is taken in faster than it is broken down or excreted, is called:
options: biodegradation
eutrophication
bioaccumulation
biomagnification
questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation happens within one organism. Biomagnification is the increase in concentration from one trophic level to the next along a food chain, which follows from bioaccumulation at each level.

questions.stem: A pollutant described as persistent is one that:
options: is released continuously from a single identifiable source such as a pipe
resists breaking down and stays in the environment for a long time
breaks down quickly into harmless products after it is released
is only toxic when it is present at very high concentrations
questions.explanation: Persistent pollutants such as DDT, PCBs and PFAS resist chemical and biological breakdown, so they last for years or decades in soil, water and organisms. Toxicity and source type are separate characteristics from persistence.

questions.stem: A persistent pesticide is measured in a lake food chain: water 0.0001 ppm, plankton 0.01 ppm, small fish 0.2 ppm, large fish 1 ppm, fish-eating birds 10 ppm. By what factor has it been magnified from small fish to birds?
questions.explanation: 10 ÷ 0.2 = 50, so the concentration in birds is 50 times that in small fish. 100 000 is the factor from the water to the birds, and 10 is the factor from large fish to birds.

questions.stem: Why does a fat-soluble, persistent pollutant such as methylmercury become most concentrated in top predators?
options: Producers make more of the pollutant by photosynthesis, which then passes up the food chain
Each consumer eats many prey and stores the pollutant, so the concentration rises at each level
Top predators drink more water than other animals, so they take in more of the dissolved pollutant
Top predators break the pollutant down more slowly because they have a faster metabolism
questions.explanation: Because the pollutant is stored in tissues rather than excreted, it is passed on in full to each consumer. A predator eats a large mass of prey over its life, so the pollutant from all of them is concentrated in its smaller body mass.

questions.stem: A persistent pollutant in soil has a half-life of 10 years. The soil currently contains 80 mg/kg. If no more is added, what concentration is expected after 30 years?
options: 0 mg/kg
10 mg/kg
20 mg/kg
40 mg/kg
questions.explanation: 30 years is three half-lives, so 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 mg/kg. 20 mg/kg is the value after two half-lives. Under exponential decay the concentration halves each period and never simply reaches zero in a fixed time.

questions.stem: In a coastal lake, the sequence of events is: fertiliser washes in, algae bloom, the algae die, oxygen falls, fish die. Which step directly causes the fall in oxygen?
options: The dead algae release toxic gases that replace dissolved oxygen
Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up dissolved oxygen
The living algae use more oxygen for photosynthesis than they make
The fertiliser reacts chemically with oxygen dissolved in the water
questions.explanation: When the bloom dies, decomposing bacteria multiply and consume large amounts of dissolved oxygen in respiration, leaving too little for fish. Photosynthesis releases oxygen rather than using it, so the living bloom actually adds oxygen during the day.

questions.stem: A sample of creek water has a high biochemical oxygen demand (BOD). What does this indicate?
options: A large amount of oxygen is dissolved in the water, so it is healthy for fish
A large population of algae is releasing oxygen into the water by photosynthesis
A large amount of salt is present, which lowers the solubility of oxygen
A large amount of organic matter is present for microorganisms to decompose
questions.explanation: BOD measures the oxygen consumed by microorganisms as they break down organic matter in a sample, so a high BOD means a heavy organic load, as from sewage or manure. It predicts low dissolved oxygen, not high, as the decomposers use it up.

questions.stem: A kick-sample upstream of a stormwater drain contains many mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly nymphs. Downstream it contains mostly worms and midge larvae. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Water quality is the same at both sites, because each site contains macroinvertebrates
Water quality cannot be judged from macroinvertebrates, so only chemical tests are useful
Water quality is likely lower downstream, as pollution-sensitive taxa are replaced by tolerant ones
Water quality is likely higher downstream, as worms and midge larvae need very clean water
questions.explanation: Mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly nymphs are sensitive to pollution and low oxygen, while worms and midge larvae tolerate poor conditions. Their replacement below the drain suggests pollution from it, which chemical tests could then confirm.

questions.stem: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released at ground level can damage the ozone layer. How do they do this?
options: They dissolve in rain, forming acids that break down ozone in the lower atmosphere
UV light in the stratosphere breaks them apart, releasing chlorine that destroys ozone
They react with ozone at ground level, which then rises to thin the ozone layer above
They trap heat in the stratosphere, which melts the ozone layer over the poles
questions.explanation: CFCs are stable enough to last for decades and drift up to the stratosphere, where UV radiation splits off chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom can destroy many ozone molecules, which is why the Montreal Protocol phased out CFC production.

questions.stem: Warm water from a power station's cooling system is discharged into a lake. Which effect on the lake is most likely?
options: Dissolved oxygen rises, because warmer water holds more gas
Salinity rises, because the warm water carries extra salts
Phosphate rises, because the heat releases it from lake sediments
Dissolved oxygen falls, stressing fish that need cooler water
questions.explanation: Thermal pollution lowers the solubility of oxygen and raises the metabolic rate, and so the oxygen need, of aquatic animals. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, not more.

questions.stem: Microplastic particles are found in the stomachs of fish far from any city. Which characteristics best explain this distribution?
options: They are biodegradable and large, so they sink quickly near their source
They are water-soluble and volatile, so they evaporate and fall in rain
They are short-lived and dense, so they settle out before reaching the sea
They are persistent and small, so they are carried long distances by currents
questions.explanation: Plastics break into smaller pieces but do not biodegrade quickly, and small, light particles are moved long distances by wind, rivers and ocean currents. Fish then mistake them for food.

questions.stem: The LD50 of a substance is:
options: the concentration that causes 50% of the substance to break down
the time taken for 50% of a test population to die
the dose that kills 50% of a test population
the dose at which 50% of a population first shows any symptoms
questions.explanation: LD50 stands for lethal dose 50%, usually given in milligrams per kilogram of body mass. A lower LD50 means less of the substance is needed to kill, so it is more toxic.

questions.stem: Pesticide X has an LD50 of 5 mg/kg and pesticide Y has an LD50 of 500 mg/kg in rats. Which statement is correct?
options: X is more acutely toxic, because a smaller dose kills half the rats
Y is more acutely toxic, because a larger dose kills half the rats
X and Y are equally toxic, because both kill half the rats
Y is more persistent in soil, because a larger dose is needed to kill
questions.explanation: The LD50 is the dose needed to kill half the test animals, so the substance with the lower LD50 is more toxic. LD50 measures acute toxicity, not how long a substance lasts in the environment.

questions.stem: A chemical has an LD50 of 40 mg/kg in a test species. What dose would be expected to kill half of a group of animals of that species with a body mass of 25 kg?
options: 65 mg
40 mg
1.6 mg
questions.explanation: The LD50 is per kilogram of body mass, so 40 mg/kg × 25 kg = 1000 mg, or 1 g. Dividing 40 by 25 gives 1.6, and 40 mg ignores the body mass altogether.

questions.stem: Health effects that appear after long-term exposure to low doses of a pollutant are described as:
options: acute toxicity
an allergic reaction
a synergistic effect
chronic toxicity
questions.explanation: Chronic toxicity results from repeated or continuous exposure over months or years, as with lead or asbestos. Acute toxicity is the effect of a single or short exposure, usually at a higher dose.

questions.stem: Exposure to two pollutants together causes far more lung damage than the sum of the damage each causes alone. This interaction is called:
options: antagonistic action
additive action
biomagnification
synergistic action
questions.explanation: In synergism the combined effect is greater than the sum of the separate effects. An additive effect equals the sum, and in antagonism one substance reduces the effect of the other.

questions.stem: A few people develop asthma-like symptoms from airborne particles at concentrations that cause no effect in most of the population. This is best explained by:
options: an allergic response in individuals sensitive to the substance
acute toxicity, because the dose is high enough to harm everyone
biomagnification of the particles in the bodies of those affected
synergistic action between the particles and the people's immune cells
questions.explanation: An allergy is an immune response to a substance that is harmless to most people, so only sensitised individuals react at low exposures. Acute toxicity would affect most people exposed to the dose.

questions.stem: A highly toxic chemical is stored in a sealed drum in a locked shed. A mildly toxic chemical is sprayed weekly in a playground. Which comparison of risk is most accurate?
options: The mildly toxic chemical may carry the greater risk, because people are often exposed to it
The highly toxic chemical always carries the greater risk, because toxicity alone sets risk
Both carry the same risk, because any chemical in the environment is equally dangerous
Neither carries any risk, because neither chemical has been released into the air
questions.explanation: Risk depends on both the hazard (toxicity) and the exposure. A sealed, locked drum gives very little exposure, while weekly spraying where children play gives frequent exposure, so the less toxic chemical may pose more risk.

questions.stem: A fish species can survive in water with dissolved oxygen above 4 mg/L but dies below this level. In terms of pollution impacts, 4 mg/L represents the species':
options: chronic exposure
synergistic threshold
tolerance limit
LD50
questions.explanation: A tolerance limit is the boundary of the conditions an organism can survive. The LD50 is a dose of a toxic substance that kills half a test group, which does not describe a minimum oxygen level.

questions.stem: Male fish downstream of a sewage outfall develop female characteristics. Tests detect synthetic hormones in the water at very low concentrations. Which impact does this show?
options: Disruption of system regulation by chemicals that mimic natural hormones
Acute toxicity, because the fish are killed quickly by a single high dose
Biomagnification, because the hormones are most concentrated in the plankton
Thermal pollution, because the outfall warms the river and changes development
questions.explanation: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals interfere with the hormone systems that regulate development and reproduction, and can act at very low doses. The fish are affected but not killed, so this is not acute toxicity.

questions.stem: Birds living beside a busy freeway sing at a noticeably higher pitch than birds of the same species in quiet bushland. Which form of pollution is most likely responsible for this change?
options: Thermal pollution
Particulate pollution
Noise pollution
Light pollution
questions.explanation: Continuous low-pitched traffic noise masks bird song, and many birds respond by singing at a higher pitch so they can still be heard when attracting mates and defending territory. Light pollution can change when birds are active, but it does not mask sound or explain a change in pitch.

questions.stem: A road raises the noise level at a nature reserve from 50 dB to 70 dB. Using the decibel scale, how many times greater is the sound intensity?
options: 20 times
1.4 times
1000 times
100 times
questions.explanation: The decibel scale is logarithmic: every 10 dB increase is a tenfold increase in intensity, so 20 dB is 10 × 10 = 100 times. 1.4 times treats the scale as linear by dividing 70 by 50.

questions.stem: Which organisation is the main regulator of pollution and waste in Victoria?
options: The Bureau of Meteorology
CSIRO
Parks Victoria
EPA Victoria
questions.explanation: EPA Victoria (the Environment Protection Authority) administers Victoria's environment protection laws, issuing licences and permits, monitoring air and water quality and enforcing the rules. CSIRO and the Bureau of Meteorology provide science and data but do not regulate pollution.

questions.stem: Under Victoria's Environment Protection Act 2017, the general environmental duty requires businesses and individuals to:
options: minimise risks of harm from pollution and waste so far as reasonably practicable
repair any pollution damage only after a court finds them to be responsible
report pollution only once it has already caused harm to human health
stop all emissions of every pollutant regardless of the cost or the risk
questions.explanation: The general environmental duty is preventive: anyone whose activities could cause harm must take reasonably practicable steps to reduce the risk before harm occurs. It does not require zero emissions at any cost, and it does not wait for harm or a court finding.

questions.stem: A network of low-cost air sensors in a city shows PM2.5 levels highest near a busy freight route on weekday mornings. How can these data best contribute to managing the pollution?
options: They show the pollution has no health impact, as it occurs only in mornings
They identify where and when exposure is highest, so action can be targeted
They prove which individual trucks are responsible, so fines can be issued
They replace the need for any regulation, as residents can now avoid the area
questions.explanation: Monitoring data reveal patterns in space and time, which helps decision-makers target measures such as rerouting trucks or setting emission standards. Area-wide sensors cannot attribute pollution to individual vehicles.

questions.stem: A council proposes banning wood heaters to improve winter air quality. Which pair of stakeholder views best shows the values in conflict?
options: All residents value cleaner air equally, so no stakeholder would oppose the proposed ban
Wood heater sellers value cleaner air; health groups value continued sales of heaters
Asthma sufferers value cleaner air; some low-income households value a cheap heating source
Asthma sufferers value cheap heating; some low-income households value cleaner winter air
questions.explanation: People with respiratory illness benefit most from reduced smoke, while households relying on firewood for affordable heat would bear the cost of a ban. Weighing such competing priorities is part of managing pollution alongside the scientific data.

questions.stem: In the waste management hierarchy, which option is the most preferred?
options: Disposing of the waste to landfill
Avoiding the creation of waste
Recycling the waste
Recovering energy from the waste
questions.explanation: The hierarchy ranks avoidance first, then reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, treat and finally dispose. Recycling is useful but still uses energy and resources, so not creating the waste in the first place is better.

questions.stem: In a wastewater treatment plant, which stage uses bacteria to break down dissolved organic matter?
options: Secondary treatment
Primary treatment
Screening
Disinfection with UV light
questions.explanation: Secondary treatment is biological: aerated tanks or lagoons let bacteria consume dissolved organic matter. Primary treatment and screening are physical, removing solids by settling and filtering, and disinfection kills pathogens at the tertiary stage.

questions.stem: Which technology is designed to remove sulfur dioxide from a coal-fired power station's exhaust gases?
options: A taller chimney that releases the gases higher into the atmosphere
A wet scrubber that passes the gases through a limestone slurry
An electrostatic precipitator that charges and collects ash particles
A catalytic converter that changes carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: In flue-gas desulfurisation, the limestone slurry reacts with sulfur dioxide to form calcium sulfate. Electrostatic precipitators remove particles, not gases, and a taller chimney only disperses the sulfur dioxide.

questions.stem: A car's catalytic converter reduces air pollution by:
options: cooling the exhaust gases so that the pollutants condense and drip out as liquid
adding oxygen to the fuel tank so that the engine produces no carbon dioxide
converting carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and unburnt fuel into less harmful gases
filtering fine particles out of the exhaust and storing them until the car is serviced
questions.explanation: Catalysts in the converter speed up reactions that turn carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides into nitrogen, and hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water. Filtering particles is a different technology, and the car still releases carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A farmer plants a strip of native grasses and shrubs between a cropped paddock and a creek. Which pollution problem does this mainly address?
options: Pesticide residues already stored in the creek's fish
Noise from the farm disturbing birds along the creek
Sediment and nutrients in run-off reaching the creek
Sulfur dioxide emissions from the farm's machinery
questions.explanation: A riparian buffer strip slows run-off so that sediment settles out, and plant roots and soil microbes take up nitrogen and phosphorus before they reach the water. It reduces diffuse pollution entering the creek, but cannot remove pesticides already in the fish.

questions.stem: Certain plants are grown on a former industrial site to absorb heavy metals from the soil, and are then harvested and removed. This treatment is called:
options: bioaccumulation
biomagnification
leaching
phytoremediation
questions.explanation: Phytoremediation uses plants to take up, stabilise or break down contaminants in soil or water. Bioaccumulation does occur inside the plants, but it describes the build-up, not the deliberate clean-up method.

questions.stem: A creek receives nitrogen and phosphorus from urban stormwater. A council compares a constructed wetland at the drain outlet with a gross pollutant trap. Which comparison is correct?
options: The trap can remove dissolved nutrients; the wetland mainly catches litter and debris
Both remove dissolved nutrients equally well, so the cheaper one should be chosen
Neither affects nutrients, because nutrients enter creeks only from farm run-off
The wetland can remove dissolved nutrients; the trap mainly catches litter and debris
questions.explanation: In a constructed wetland, plants and microbes take up and transform nitrogen and phosphorus while sediment settles. A gross pollutant trap is a screen or basket that captures solid litter, leaves and debris, but dissolved nutrients pass straight through it.

questions.stem: After an oil spill on a beach, nutrients are added to encourage naturally occurring bacteria to break down the oil. This approach is called:
options: incineration
containment
bioremediation
phytoremediation
questions.explanation: Bioremediation uses microorganisms to break pollutants into less harmful substances, and adding nutrients speeds up their growth. Phytoremediation uses plants rather than microorganisms.
